title: Opening and context
short: Probably written in 1802-04, published in Poems, in Two Volumes (1807); 'the world' is worldly, commercial life, which presses on us constantly.
body: The sonnet belongs to the outburst of sonnets Wordsworth wrote from 1802, when he took up Milton's Petrarchan model. It appeared among the 'Miscellaneous Sonnets' in 1807. 'The world' has the moral sense of the New Testament: 'Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world' (1 John 2:15), meaning the realm of material interests set against spiritual life. 'Too much with us' means it occupies us excessively. 'Late and soon' (late and early) means at all times, an older idiom.

sources.cite: Jared Curtis, ed., Poems, in Two Volumes, and Other Poems, 1800-1807 (Cornell Wordsworth, 1983)

title: Getting and spending
short: Earning and buying exhaust our faculties; commercial life wastes our human powers.
body: The participles describe a cycle of acquisition and consumption that critics often relate to Britain's expanding commercial and industrial economy around 1800. 'Lay waste our powers' uses a military idiom (to lay waste a country) for self-destruction; 'powers' means the faculties of feeling and imagination. The thought parallels the Preface to Lyrical Ballads, which complains that city life and the craving for stimulation blunt 'the discriminating powers of the mind'.

title: Little we see in Nature that is ours
short: We have lost our sense of belonging to the natural world; nature no longer seems ours.
body: The line inverts the economic language of possession: in the age of getting, we own much and yet cannot claim nature, which requires a different kind of relationship. The capital N personifies Nature, as in 'Tintern Abbey'. The line anticipates the speaker's turn to paganism, a religion in which nature was felt to be full of gods, so that every sea and meadow had its presiding deity.

title: a sordid boon
short: An oxymoron: we have given away our hearts, and the gift (boon) is a base, mercenary one.
body: A 'boon' is a gift or favour, often one granted on request; 'sordid' (Latin sordidus, dirty) means mean, mercenary or degraded. Editors debate the syntax: the phrase can describe the act of giving our hearts away (a squalid bargain) or what we received in exchange (worldly goods, a contemptible reward). Either way, the oxymoron sums up the bad bargain of a commercial society. The semicolon after it closes the octave's first half, the diagnosis.

anchor: bares her bosom to the moon
title: This Sea that bares her bosom to the moon
short: The sea is personified as a woman baring her breast to the moon, an image of intimacy and natural attraction that leaves us unmoved.
body: The image combines erotic personification with natural fact, the moon's pull on the tides. The winds that 'will be howling at all hours' are now 'up-gathered... like sleeping flowers', folded in calm, a simile that domesticates wildness. These are examples of the natural grandeur we fail to feel. The capital in 'Sea' marks a further personification, preparing for the sea-gods of the sestet.

title: out of tune
short: We are not attuned to nature: a musical metaphor for lost harmony.
body: The metaphor of tuning suggests an instrument that no longer responds to the world, compare the Aeolian harp, a favourite Romantic image for a mind responsive to natural influences (Coleridge, 'The Eolian Harp'). 'For this, for everything' broadens the charge from these sights to all of nature. The line ends the octave, in which the speaker speaks for 'us'; in the sestet he speaks as 'I'.

title: Petrarchan sonnet with displaced volta
short: A Petrarchan sonnet (abbaabba cdcdcd) in which the turn comes mid-line, after 'It moves us not', with a sudden outburst.
body: The octave runs on into line 9 with a short, flat sentence that sums up the complaint; the volta then arrives in mid-line with the exclamation 'Great God!' This displaced turn imitates Milton's sonnets, which often break the octave-sestet division, and gives a sense of rising passion. The rhymes in the octave (soon/boon/moon/... powers/hours/flowers) are tight; the sestet alternates (be/lea/sea; outworn/forlorn/horn).

title: A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn
short: He would rather be raised in an obsolete pagan religion, if it let him feel nature's divinity.
body: A 'Pagan' (Latin paganus, a country-dweller, later a non-Christian) is one outside the Christian faith. 'Suckled' means nursed from infancy, so the belief would be bred in the bone. 'Creed outworn' admits the pagan faith is dead. The outburst is shocking from a Christian poet, though the conditional 'I'd rather be' marks it as a rhetorical preference rather than a statement of belief. Comparable nostalgia for Greek religion appears in Schiller's 'Die Götter Griechenlandes' (1788) and later in Keats.

title: pleasant lea
short: A lea is a meadow or grassland; the phrase echoes Spenser.
body: 'Lea' (Old English leah, a clearing or meadow) is a poetic word for open grassland, here near the sea. Wordsworth's editors note the echo of Spenser's Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), l. 283, 'Yet seemed to be a goodly pleasant lea'. Spenser's poem also supplies the image of Triton in the final line, so the sestet has a Spenserian frame: it imagines the pagan world through the lens of Elizabethan mythological pastoral.

title: Proteus
short: Proteus is the shape-changing old man of the sea in Homer and Virgil, herdsman of Poseidon's seals.
body: In Odyssey Book 4 Menelaus seizes Proteus on the shore of Pharos and holds him through all his transformations until he prophesies; Virgil retells the story with Aristaeus in Georgics 4. As a god of the sea's changing forms and of prophecy, Proteus embodies the living, divine nature the modern world cannot see. 'Have sight of' answers 'Little we see' in line 3. Spenser's Colin Clout passage also pairs Proteus with Triton among the sea-gods.

anchor: old Triton blow his wreathèd horn
title: Triton and his wreathèd horn
short: Triton, son of Poseidon, blows a conch shell to calm or rouse the seas; the line echoes Spenser and Ovid.
body: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (1.330-42) Neptune orders Triton to blow his shell-trumpet to call back the flood waters after the deluge. Spenser's Colin Clout (l. 245) has 'Triton blowing loud his wreathed horne', which Wordsworth's line closely follows. 'Wreathèd' means spirally twisted, like a conch; the accent tells the reader to pronounce it as two syllables, keeping the pentameter. The poem ends on a sound, so the speaker's wish moves from sight to hearing, a full sensory renewal.
